items.q: Which is an authentication failure (OWASP A07)?
options: Letting users pick a long passphrase
Expiring sessions after inactivity
Offering multi-factor authentication
Storing passwords in plain text and allowing unlimited login guesses with no lockout

explain.right: Plaintext passwords plus unlimited guessing are classic authentication failures; fixes are password-specific hashing, rate limiting/lockout, and MFA.
explain.wrong: Long passphrases, MFA, and session expiry are all good practices, not failures.

items.q: How should user passwords be stored?
options: As a fast plain SHA-256 hash with no salt
In plain text, but in a private database
Hashed with a slow, salted, password-specific algorithm (e.g. bcrypt or argon2)
Encrypted with the same key used for everything else

explain.right: Use a slow, salted algorithm built for passwords (bcrypt/argon2) so stolen hashes resist cracking; never store plaintext.
explain.wrong: Plaintext is indefensible, a shared reversible key is risky, and fast unsalted SHA-256 is crackable at scale.

items.q: Which best describes security misconfiguration (OWASP A02)?
options: A user choosing a weak password
A bug in the application's logic
A slow database query
An insecure setup — e.g. debug mode on in production, default passwords unchanged, or a storage bucket left public

explain.right: Misconfiguration is an insecure setup rather than a code bug: defaults, verbose errors, open storage, unused features left on.
explain.wrong: It's distinct from app logic bugs, weak user passwords (A07), and performance issues.

items.q: Your code is clean, but you use a library with a known critical vulnerability. Under OWASP 2025 this is:
options: Software supply chain failure (A03) — you inherit the security of every dependency, so you must track and update them
Not your problem — it's the library author's fault
Only a risk if you call that exact function
Safe because the library is popular

explain.right: Dependencies are part of your attack surface; a vulnerable library is your risk. Use lockfiles, dependency alerts/SCA, and update promptly.
explain.wrong: Blame doesn't reduce exposure, popularity doesn't equal safety, and a vulnerable dependency can be reachable in ways you didn't expect.

items.q: Which pairing of a 2025 OWASP risk with its defense is correct?
options: Security Logging and Alerting Failures → log security-relevant events AND alert on the suspicious ones so breaches don't go unnoticed
Insecure Design → add the security checks after launch once the design is proven
Cryptographic Failures → invent your own encryption algorithm for extra secrecy
Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions → on an error, fail open and let the request through to avoid annoying users

explain.right: Logging without alerting lets breaches sit unnoticed; you log auth/access events and alert on the suspicious ones (A09).
explain.wrong: Never roll your own crypto (A04), fail closed not open on errors (A10), and design security in early — some flaws can't be patched later (A06).
